content.text:
The installer can report a successful Scoop installation while an older binary remains active, and direct PowerShell installations are not integrated with the existing update mechanism. It also mishandles valid drive-root installation paths.

Full review comments:

- [P2] Check PATH conflicts after Scoop installs — /Users/gtrrz-victor/wks/cli/uninstall-ext/scripts/install.ps1:287-290
  When a stable install uses Scoop while an older direct installation appears earlier on `PATH`, this early return skips all conflict detection. The script reports success, but `entire` still resolves to the older executable. Verify the resolved command after the Scoop install and warn or fail when the Scoop shim does not take priority.

- [P2] Teach version checks about direct PowerShell installs — /Users/gtrrz-victor/wks/cli/uninstall-ext/scripts/install.ps1:371-374
  For nightly installs and stable installs without Scoop, this writes the executable to a path that `installManagerForCurrentBinary` classifies as unknown. On Windows, `canAutoInstall` consequently returns false because it still assumes no native installer exists, so update notifications show only the releases page instead of the new channel-preserving PowerShell command. Add detection and update commands for this installation method.

- [P2] Preserve drive roots when normalizing install paths — /Users/gtrrz-victor/wks/cli/uninstall-ext/scripts/install.ps1:205-208
  When `-InstallDir` is a drive root such as `C:\`, `TrimEnd` converts it to `C:`, which Windows interprets as the current directory on that drive rather than its root. The installer can therefore copy the binaries into an unrelated working directory. Avoid trimming the separator when the normalized path is a volume root.

I’ll use the diagnose workflow to trace each review finding into the installer and update logic, then add focused regression coverage. I’m also applying the repo’s required writing cleanup skill to the final handoff.
